newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk PM Erbakan signs army warning to Islamists.
newsitem.headline: Turk PM Erbakan signs army warning to Islamists.

text.p: Turkey's military-dominated National Security Council (NSC) said on Wednesday that Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan had signed a council statement demanding a crackdown on religious activism.

Erbakan had initially refused to sign the warning, appealing for political solidarity and arguing that democracy meant his government answered only to parliament and not the army, but other political leaders had refused to heed his plea.

"(The NSC statement) was signed by Prime Minister Erbakan without any changes," the council's secretary general, Ilhan Kilic, was quoted as saying by state-run Anatolian news agency on leaving the prime ministry.
Erbakan's decision ended an apparent deadlock between the military -- which three times over the past 37 years has overthrown democratically elected governments -- and his coalition government.

The council, dominated by the powerful military, demanded in a weekend statement that Erbakan's coalition crack down on religious activism, which the NSC said was largely fostered by his Islam-based Welfare Party.
"The signature, the crisis...these problems have been completely overcome," Kilic told reporters after half-an-hour of talks with Erbakan.
The apparent deadlock had put strains on Erbakan's coalition with Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller's conservative, secular True Path Party and sent shares tumbling 15 percent in Turkey this week.

The Istanbul share index closed 4.92 percent lower on the day in political uncertainty following the security council warning. Bond yields were also up sharply on Wednesday, jumping 6-8 percentage points to around 110 percent.

Traders said there was widespread concern in the markets that the political turmoil would distract government attention away from addressing the deep-seated problems of an economy struggling 80 percent annual inflation and wide deficits.
Ciller had suggested the crisis could also damage the country's chances of joining the European Union. She planned to lobby ambassadors from EU countries on Thursday.
"To be successful we need a continuation of stability," she told reporters. "The continuation of the secular Turkish republic and democracy are very important. A shadow should not be cast on them."
Ministers from Erbakan's eight-month-old coalition were to meet on Thursday for a cabinet meeting.
Long-held dreams of a place in the European Union received a public blow on Tuesday, when leading EU figures spoke out against Turkey's membership. It now has associate member status.

Turkey's three biggest trade unions, meanwhile, said the army's move to quell alleged Islamist separatism had the full support of their six million members. Leftist leaders told told Erbakan the same thing on Tuesday.

Mainstream newspapers and television channels have joined the chorus of approval for the NSC, with some even urging the army to topple the government. Nightly street demonstrations have increasingly targetted the Islamists.
This groundswell behind the military chiefs reflects widespread respect for the armed forces among Turkey's secular majority as a bulwark against religious extremism.
"Modern, secular democracy is in danger," said the chiefs of three big unions in a joint letter to party leaders. "This is why we support the National Security Council decisions."
